topic: grafting an old apple variety onto seedling rootstocks and renewal pruning a neglected pear

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-2)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: termometr przymrozkowy z zapisem minimum

base: I am grafting scions from an old apple variety onto seedling rootstocks in the bottom orchard.
An old pear tree stands at the top of the same slope and fruits every second year.
A frost thermometer hangs among the trees and keeps the lowest reading of each night.
My whip graft looks neat enough, though the cambium only meets along one side of the cut.
Does that matter much, or will the union close anyway once the sap begins to rise?
One good side of contact is enough, provided you bind it firmly and seal every opening.
Cambium meeting on both sides simply gives you two chances instead of one, nothing more.
Bind from below upwards so rain runs off the tape rather than into the joint.
Then wax the top of the scion, because most failures come from drying, not from cold.
I bound and waxed twelve grafts and eight of them have pushed strong shoots already.
Three did nothing at all and one pushed briefly before wilting in the first warm week.
The frost thermometer recorded minus four on two nights just after I finished the grafting.
The old pear tree was in full blossom then and lost most of its flowers.
Would that frost alone kill a fresh union, or does the wilting point to something else?
Minus four will not kill a bound graft, since the union sits under tape and wax.
A graft that pushes and then wilts has almost always dried out at the join.
Check whether the tape loosened, because a small gap lets wind take the moisture out.
Losing pear blossom to the same frost tells you nothing about wood that is still dormant.
The tape on the failed grafts had indeed worked loose near the top of the scion.
I rebound the survivors more tightly and every one of them is still growing well.
Now the shoots are a foot long and beginning to lean away from the stem.
Should I stake each shoot, or cut them back to encourage a stronger union first?
Stake them and leave the length alone, because a growing shoot feeds the union below.
Cutting back now slows the very growth that thickens the joint through the first summer.
Tie the shoot to a cane above and below the graft to stop wind rocking it.
Take the tape off in late summer, or it will strangle the stem as it swells.
I staked every shoot and removed the tape in August exactly as you described.
The unions have swollen nicely and none of the shoots snapped in the autumn gales.
Now I am wondering about the old pear tree, which has not been pruned for years.
Its centre is a thicket of upright shoots and the fruit hangs only on the outside.
Renewal pruning takes three winters, because taking that much wood at once invites more thicket.
Remove one third of the crowded branches this year, choosing the oldest and most upright.
Cut back to a side branch rather than leaving stubs, which only sprout again quickly.
Then wait a full season and judge what the tree has done before touching it again.
I took out the worst third last winter and the tree has responded fairly calmly.
There are fewer upright shoots this year and the fruit reaches further into the centre.
The pears themselves are small, though, and many of them drop before they ripen properly.
Is that a thinning problem, or does the tree carry more fruit than it can feed?
It carries far more than it can feed, which is normal for a neglected tree.
Thin the young fruit in June to one per cluster, hard as that always feels.
The tree then puts everything into what remains instead of dropping half the crop.
Feed the ground with rotted manure in autumn and expect real improvement in the third year.
